review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

High electrical conductivity is crucial for electrics, electronics, communications. Eliminating defects such as grain boundaries and impurities is a primary approach to enhancing electrical conductivity in metals. Although reducing electron-phonon interaction can further contribute to electrical conductivity, only a marginal enhancement is obtained by imposing external pressure even high up to gigapascal. Here we report a contrary strategy to transforming defects into conductive benefits, by forming abundant defects of severely distorted lattice via heterogeneous interface-assisted plastic deformation in metal (copper). Such lattice distortions are generated under a non-extreme condition, and cause internal giant local stress significantly suppressing electron-phonon coupling and thus reducing phonon-caused electron scattering. Consequently, a striking bulk electrical conductivity of >110% IACS is obtained in the copper at room temperature, which is equivalent to the effect of an external high pressure of about 10 gigapascals. Our work provides an extendable approach for developing high-performance metal conductors.

---

## Introduction

Electrical energy is the main form of energy transport and conversion. The development of high-performance conductor materials has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of systems and devices, reduce energy consumption, and increase integration and power density. Taking an example, the electrical conductivity of interconnects exceeding that of pure copper can effectively improve signal transmission rate, reduce bit error rate, and chip power consumption1–5. According to Matthiessen’s rule, electron scattering caused by phonon and lattice defects, including vacancies, grain boundaries (GBs), impurities, and dislocations, collectively deteriorates electrical conductivity in metals1,6–8. To minimize the deleterious effects of the above electron scattering factors on electrical conductivity, a multitude of methods have been employed, such as increasing lattice integrity and inhibiting grain refinement, as well as purification.

Copper is the most widely used metal conductor material owing to its high conductivity and low cost. However, a very limited increment in the electrical conductivity of Cu has been achieved since the International Annealed Copper Standard (IACS, electrical conductivity of Cu is 100% IACS) was established in 1913. For example, electrical conductivity is less than 103% IACS in oxygen-free Cu with a purity as high as 7N-level, and ~110% IACS in Cu single crystal without GBs9,10. In recent years, some explorations have shown the potential in improving electrical conductivity to a higher level by forming composites either in bulk or on surface2,11–13, and the enhancement of electrical conductivity was mainly attributed to the doping effect, reducing electron scattering on the Cu–C interface, enhancing thermal heat dissipation, etc. But most of the above strategies do not alter the intrinsic electrical conductivity of the metal matrix.

Essentially, the intrinsic electrical conductivity of some phase is dominated by its electronic structure and energy band, which can be influenced by applying external fields, including force, temperature, and magnetism, etc., leading to some strategies such as strain engineering and band engineering14–17. For example, the compression-shear stress on diamond changed charge redistribution and softened phonon, resulting in the production of robust superconductivity18. Regarding metals, it was proved that applying pressure on Cu can suppress electron-phonon coupling (EPC) and thus improve its electrical conductivity, but a very limited increment by 2% was achieved19 when subject to high pressure, even up to 2 gigapascal (GPa). Moreover, in most cases, these benefits are not integrated as intrinsic properties of the materials, and they disappear as the applied fields are removed.

Contrary to the conventional wisdom of eliminating structural defects, we proposed introducing nanolayers of severely distorted copper lattice at GBs in nanograined Cu to act as highly conductive channels by means of suppressing electron-phonon interaction strength and reducing phonon-caused electron scattering. The local giant stress is caused by accumulated copious strain energy upon cold drawing (ε≈12) and subsequent annealing-induced anisotropic expansion due to the thermal expansion coefficient (TEC) mismatch between the Cu matrix and strained graphene at GBs. Additionally, it has high thermal stability (at least up to 773K), and no external extreme fields are required to maintain it.

---

## Results

Fabrication and ultra high electrical conductivity
To obtain sufficient deformability and grain refinement to the nanoscale simultaneously, we incorporated trace graphene (Supplementary Note 1, about several tens of parts per million in volume fraction) at GBs to assist plastic deformation of coarse-grained Cu20. The ultimate nanograined Cu wires were obtained through a sequential process involving in-situ growth of graphene on Cu foils (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1), laminated structure assembling, hot-pressing molding, hot extrusion, and cold drawing, followed by a subsequent thermal annealing treatment in the final step (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2). Such trace graphene at GBs enables Cu exceptional plastic deformability, i.e. the extruded bar (diameter d=13 mm) can be continuously cold drawn to wires (d<0.03 mm) without intermediate thermal annealing (corresponding to a strain of ~12, Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Because of the constraint role of graphene at GBs, Cu samples containing trace graphene (Gr–Cu) have stronger ability on grain refinement and higher thermal stability than that without graphene inside (Fig. 1b, f, Supplementary Fig. 4, and Supplementary Fig. 5). After thermal annealing treatment, with the same diameters (d≈0.4 mm), grain size coarsened up to ~50±13.4 μm in the pure Cu wire (Fig. 1b), much larger than the value of ~0.72±0.21 μm in the Gr–Cu wire (Fig. 1c). As the drawing process continued, nanograined structures were formed and retained in the final cold drawn Gr–Cu wires and annealed Gr–Cu wires, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12 and Fig. 1d–f).

We compared the electrical conductivities of Gr–Cu wires and Cu wires prepared using the same raw materials and method (Fig. 1g and Supplementary Fig. 6). For pure Cu wires, as expected, their electrical conductivities decrease gradually with increasing strain, and slightly recover upon thermal annealing treatment. In contrast, the electrical conductivity of the Gr–Cu wires remains almost unchanged in the whole process of cold drawing, and witnessed drastic increases after thermal annealing treatment, with a certified exceptional electrical conductivity larger than 110% IACS (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 7), which is more than 10% higher than that of pure Cu. It is worth emphasizing that, contradictory to the conventional belief that as the grain size is refined to nanometer scale, the electrical conductivity will significantly decrease21,22, the electrical conductivity inversely increases with decreasing grain size in the plastically deformed Gr–Cu here (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 8). Our findings strongly suggested that grain refinement not always decreases electrical conductivity, which contradicts the notion established in conventional materials.

While Ag is well known as the best electrical conductor among all the metals, the Gr–Cu here shows comprehensive advantages over Ag as indicated by the expanded area in the performance radar chart (Fig. 1j). Ag has higher electrical conductivity than Cu, but Cu is used in much larger quantities because Ag is too expensive. The Gr–Cu material provides an attractive choice with electrical conductivity higher than Ag but price around Cu. Moreover, pure Cu has a higher current-carrying capacity than Ag, and incorporating graphene will further improve this performance23,24, indicating higher power and safety in applications. Additionally, the density of Gr–Cu is almost the same as that of pure Cu, about 85% that of Ag, implying direct benefit for lightweighting in practical devices and systems. In many applications, high electrical conductivity and high mechanical strength are often required simultaneously, but methods used to strengthen metals generally also cause a pronounced decrease in electrical conductivity1. Fortunately, the Gr–Cu material has both higher electrical conductivity and mechanical strength than either Cu or Ag, which provides a pathway to develop high-performance metal conductors.

Nanostructure formation and lattice distortion
In the as-sintered Gr–Cu sample, a micro-laminated structure was observed, and the lamellae thickness of ~25 μm is close to the thickness of the raw Cu foils and the as-prepared Gr–Cu foils (Supplementary Fig. 9), implying that the inter-lamella graphene inhibited across-lamella grain coarsening in the process of hot-pressing sintering. By subsequent hot extrusion and multi-pass cold drawing, the few-layer graphene at GBs was thinned and further dispersed via shear-induced interlayer sliding (Supplementary Fig. 10 and Supplementary Video 1), and plays the role of inhibiting dynamic recovery and recrystallization against plastic deformation. As a result, the lamellae were continuously thinned and finally refined to the nanoscale (Supplementary Fig. 11).

As the diameter of the Gr–Cu wire reached ~50 μm (corresponding to a strain of ~11), the average lamellar thickness is about 100 nm (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 11). Such graphene-assisted deformation has a prominent ability for grain refinement, and differs from the conventional refining mechanism dominated by dislocation slip in pure Cu under moderate deformation conditions25,26. The kernel averaged misorientation (KAM) map (Fig. 2b) suggests high misorientation within grains in the as-drawn Gr–Cu wire (d≈50 μm), i.e., a high density of dislocations was accumulated, and copious strain energy was stored inside after cold drawing. Nanotwins are also observed as penetrating through the Cu lamellae with a twin/matrix thickness of ~10 nm (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 12).

Thermal annealing treatment is the only process resulting in the remarkable enhancement of conductivity, and we compared microstructure change in the annealed Gr–Cu wire (d≈50 μm) (Fig. 2d–g). The nanolaminated structure remained after annealing, and the grains slightly coarsened to an average grain size of 175±138 nm. As a noticeable difference from the as-drawn sample, the annealed sample shows much weaker intragranular misorientation, while strong misorientation concentrates along the lamellar boundary or the Gr–Cu interface (Fig. 2e). These observations imply that the stored strain was redistributed upon thermal annealing. Under high-resolution TEM (HRTEM), we found nanolayers with a clear contrast exist along boundary or interface (Fig. 2f), and corresponding geometrical phase analysis (GPA) shows obvious lattice strain in the nanolayers of Cu matrix (Fig. 2g). Carefully examination of the interplanar spacing of the Cu(111) in the distorted region was changed by ~10% (indicated by the blue and yellow box in Supplementary Fig. 13d).

Furthermore, we estimated the lattice strain by performing synchrotron X-ray micro-diffraction (μ-XRD) (with a wavelength of 0.563 Å and a spot size of ~5 μm) on both the as-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu wire samples (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 14). The 1-D patterns integrated from the Debye-Scherrer rings27,28 are shown in a 2θ angle range from 10° to 35°. The diffraction peaks at the 2θ angles of 15.5°, 17.9°, 25.5°, 29.9°, and 31.3° correspond to the (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222) planes of Cu, respectively. The as-drawn sample has diffraction peaks with a typical symmetrical profile, indicating homogeneous microstructure and strain distribution (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Fig. 15). Usually, thermal annealing treatment can reduce lattice defects and promote crystallinity, resulting in sharper diffraction peaks29,30. However, some abnormal changes were observed in the μ-XRD patterns of the annealed Gr–Cu sample. After annealing, while the diffraction peak intensities increase significantly, asymmetrical broadening at varying degrees takes place in the peak profiles, typically as shown at the foot of the peaks at low diffraction angles. More μ-XRD patterns with varying features of peak broadening and also some extra peaks are shown in Supplementary Fig. 15. We excluded any possible contribution from impurities to such unusual changes in diffraction patterns because (1) graphene and Cu are immiscible with each other, (2) no oxides were detected by checking peak positions and using electron energy loss spectroscopy. Moreover, the thermal annealing treatment was carried out in an inert atmosphere, and μ-XRD was performed on the polished fresh surface. Hence, we believe that such asymmetrical broadening of peaks was caused by anisotropic strain31 and thus inhomogeneous lattice distortion of the copper lattice in the annealed Gr–Cu wires. Based on the Scherrer equation, we can roughly estimate the type and degree of such observed lattice distortion according to the peak positions, either expansion or compression of interplanar spacing32,33. Lattice compression distortion was mainly reflected by the asymmetrical broadening on the right foot side of some diffraction peaks, with a typical broadening width of about 1~2° for 2θ, indicating that the corresponding interplanar spacing was compressed by ~5% (see Supplementary Note 3 for further details).

Microstructure evolution inducing local strain
To explore the microstructure evolution and formation of lattice distortion during annealing, we conducted in-situ heating experiments in TEM. The low-magnification TEM images revealed that the nanolaminated structure was thermally stable during in-situ heating (Supplementary Fig. 16 and Supplementary Video 2). Closer observations in HRTEM (Fig. 3a–d) show some meaningful details on microstructure evolution. In the randomly selected nanolamella (about 50 nm in width) in the TEM specimen cut from the as-drawn Gr–Cu wire, dense strain moiré fringes were observed in the lamellae before heating34,35. As the heating temperature increased, the strained zone became narrower gradually, and the fringes in the middle region of the nanolamella disappeared ultimately, which seems like the strain was concentrating towards GBs on two sides upon heating. As revealed by HRTEM, two nanolayers with clear contrast and compressive strain (εxy) formed along the GBs on both sides (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Video 3), which is consistent with the features of microstructure and nanolayers as observed in the ex-situ annealed Gr–Cu samples (Fig. 2f).

We also conducted Raman measurements of graphene in the interface to estimate the interfacial stress (Fig. 3e). We observed a slight blue shift of the Raman G peak after sintering (without deformation), and a larger shift to higher wavenumbers in the as-extruded Gr–Cu sample (with an extrusion ratio of 9.5 and a strain ε≈2.2). Raman peak position can be used as the index of strain state in graphene; a significant red shift of ~14.2 cm−1 per 1% strain for Raman G peak was observed in graphene under uniaxial tensile strain36. In contrast to the tensile strain, the reported in-plane biaxial compression-induced blue shifts37 of the Raman G peak for the graphite or graphene vary from 4.1 to 4.9 cm−1·GPa−1. Compared to pristine graphene38 or our graphene transferred from Gr/Cu foil to silicon substrate, the blue shift of the Raman G peak in the as-extruded sample is estimated to be around 30 cm−1 in our work. Thus, it can be approximately calculated that the compressive stress caused a shift of the G peak of 6.1–7.3 GPa. It is reasonable to expect that even more significant Raman shifts and thus actual stress much larger than 8 GPa in the annealed Gr–Cu wires (the strain ε as high as 12 in the wire with d<0.03 mm), although it is challenging to further collect Raman spectra for the highly dispersed graphene in the Cu matrix.

This interfacial stress induced by the TEC mismatch between the severely strained graphene and Cu matrix was elucidated in Fig. 3f. Upon elevating temperature during sintering and annealing, along the direction parallel to the nanolamella, graphene contracted due to its negative TEC in-plane39 while the Cu matrix oppositely expanded. Subsequently, graphene tends to expand while Cu tends to shrink, resulting in the formation of graphene wrinkles (described as ripples or folds) during the cooling process. The interfacial compressive stress was partially released by forming folds or ripples40,41, while the majority of the compressive stress was still retained, resulting in a biaxial compressive stress on the Cu matrix. In the other direction, perpendicular to the nanolamella, graphene itself expanded and also constrained the expansion of the Cu matrix, thus leading to a uniaxial compressive stress. Consequently, a multi-directional compressive stress formed near the Cu–C interface, which is consistent with that reported in the graphene/Cu micro-laminated composites42. However, only in the drawn Gr–Cu wire does such a compressive stress effect contribute to a substantial increase in bulk electrical conductivity. Firstly, copious strain energy was accumulated in the process of cold drawing, and graphene was highly strained, resulting in a larger compressive stress generated at the Cu–C interface. Additionally, the proportion of the strain-affected area becomes large enough as the Cu lamellae are refined to the nanoscale. For instance, the width of the distorted nanolayer ranged from 5 to 20 nm for the nanolamellae with a thickness of ~50 nm in Figs. 2f and 3d. Such microstructure evolution and strain accumulation can well explain the strain-dependent enhancement of electrical conductivity (Fig. 1g, h).

Giant stress in the annealed Gr–Cu wire was also confirmed by severe lattice distortion of copper, as shown in the atomic-scale images of the nanolayer (Fig. 3g, h) collected by high-resolution high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) imaging in an aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM). As shown in Fig. 3g, we clearly identify a distinctive torsion of the (111) planes. In addition, a typical expansion of (200) interplanar spacing increased by ~27%, from ~1.80 Å to ~2.29 Å in the distorted nanolayer was observed (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 18), which was confirmed by some extra peaks around 2θ of ~14° in the μ-XRD patterns (inset, Supplementary Fig. 16). Further first-principles calculations indicated that such a large lattice expansion requires local stress of several tens of GPa. We have also conducted molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the maintaining effect of graphene on the mechanical properties of the graphene-reinforced copper composites and stable interfacial bonding (Supplementary Fig. 19). The results show the remarkable increase in the tensile strength due to the hindering effect on the dislocations. Especially, comparing with the microstructure at a strain of ~0.5, the microstructure at a strain of ~0.7 was kept stable without interfacial separation. Additionally, the detachment phenomena are less likely to occur under compressive loading43. Thus, based on the above experimental and MD results, interfacial compressive stress was induced and kept without interfacial separation.

Suppression of EPC
Strain-tuning electrically conductive performance was further elucidated by conducting first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 20). The EPC constant λ and Eliashberg spectral function α2F(ω) were obtained. The calculated λ is 0.124 for copper under unstrained conditions. This is in good agreement with the previously reported value41 of 0.14. As the compressive strain increased to 2%, 5%, and 10%, the corresponding calculated λ decreased to 0.113, 0.095, and 0.07, 8 respectively. We also noticed that the spectral functions were shifted to higher frequencies after applying strain, and the intensities of the peaks were reduced, resulting in weakening the scattering effects on electrons. Thus, according to the calculated Eliashberg spectral function α2F(ω) and frequency-dependent EPC λ(ω), we can infer that the electron-phonon interaction strength was reduced after applying strain19,44. As the lattice strain can be determined to be ~5% from the μ-XRD diffraction patterns, a pressure of ~30 GPa was required to achieve a similar lattice strain in the above DFT-calculated hydrostatic pressure. Similar compressive strain increasing the conductivity was also confirmed using experimental tests and simulated calculations in the copper/graphene composites45. Besides, it was recently proposed that the electrical resistivity decreases in aluminum and copper wires upon pressuring each metal19 (Supplementary Fig. 21d). If the graphene-wrapped nanograin in the Supplementary Fig. 21c is analogized to a copper wire, its compressive stress state is similar to that reported in the literature19. Moreover, similar experimental and simulation results on compressive stress suppressing EPC to enhance the conductivity of Au have also been reported in our recent work46. Theory calculations reveal that ~60% increment of electrical conductivity can be achieved at ~30 GPa for the metals of silver and gold47. Göran Grimvall48 systematically investigated the effects of electron-phonon interaction (λ) on the electronic properties and electrical performance, and concluded that λ for the noble metals is well within the approximate limits 0.07–0.24 (Cu), 0.05–0.25 (Ag), and 0.07–0.26 (Au). Besides, a similar recommended value for the Cu, Ag, and Au of ~0.14 was given. Moreover, the ratio of resistivity to temperature (ρ/T) can be used to describe the scattering of conduction electrons by thermal vibrations, and the trend of Cu is close to that of Ag49. As shown in Fig. 2d, 20% nanostructured grains remained in the annealed Gr–Cu wire due to the Cu–C interface. Consequently, we estimated the average electrical conductivity of ~112% IACS according to the rule of mixtures. This is in close agreement with our measurement results of ~110% IACS for the bulk Gr–Cu samples. For comparison purposes, we also accommodated graphene into the DFT model and carried out the corresponding calculations in Supplementary Fig. 22. The calculated λ is 0.171 for the Gr–Cu composite model under unstrained conditions. As the compressive strain increased to 5%, the corresponding calculated λ decreased to 0.137. The variation is about 0.034, which is generally close to that of the FCC copper cell. Considering the distribution of graphene in the Gr–Cu wires and the interfacial compressive stress, graphene was employed as a medium to cause internal giant local stress, resulting in significantly suppressing EPC and enhancing electrical conductivity. Thus, the DFT model of the FCC copper cell could be more suitable to simulate the experimental results.

This suppression of EPC was further confirmed by the measured temperature-dependent resistivity curves of cold-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu composite wires from 3 to 300 K using the physical property measurement system (PPMS) (Fig. 4b). The resistivity of the cold-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu wires at 293 K was 1.67 μΩ·cm and 1.54 μΩ·cm, respectively. This is roughly consistent with the results measured using macroscopic samples in Fig. 1g. As shown in Fig. 4b, the electrical resistivity of the two samples decreased linearly with the temperature down to 100 K. Subsequently, the two curves showed nonlinear trends below 100 K until close to horizontal. It is found that the residual resistivity (ρ0) of the as-drawn sample is 1.75±0.05×10−2 μΩ·cm, which is close to the values (0.51×10−2 μΩ·cm) of the oxygen-free copper (OFC) and the values (0.33×10−2 μΩ·cm) of the single-crystal copper (SCC) in the literature10,21. The residual resistivity values (6.75±0.04×10−2 μΩ·cm) of the annealed sample are larger than those of the as-drawn sample. According to Boltzmann transport theory, the residual resistivity caused by defect scattering is temperature independent50,51. It suggests that the annealed sample contains more defects than that in the cold-drawn sample. Furthermore, the measured temperature coefficient of resistivity at 293 K was ~6.7×10−11 K−1 for the cold-drawn Gr–Cu sample. This matches well with the value of 6.8×10−11 K−1 for the oxygen-free high conductivity (OFHC) Cu52. As a comparison, it was ~5.9×10−11 K−1 for the annealed Gr–Cu sample, which is ~12% lower than that of cold drawn sample. These results indicate that the EPC was suppressed at moderate temperature in the annealed Gr–Cu sample due to the distorted nanolayer.

Our observations indicate that abundant GBs with a distorted lattice in the nanograined Cu enable an exceptional electrical conductivity and also comprehensive properties outperforming those of bulk Ag. Such a property enhancement differs fundamentally from that of the traditional strategies, lying in structural integrity and phase purity. Reduction in the electron–phonon interaction strength by introducing lattice distortion through conventional plastic deformation can be emerged as an intrinsic property of materials, making not only the effect more significant but also extreme external conditions unnecessary, such as high pressure. Our findings also demonstrate that grain refinement (a typical method to enhance strength) does not always lead to a decrease in electrical conductivity, combining strengthening with a second phase (graphene here), which provides an effective approach to enhance electrical conductivity and mechanical strength simultaneously, which has been a long-standing challenge in materials science. Such a strategy, achieving many objectives at one stroke, could also be feasibly applied to many other 2D-material/metal systems, particularly toward the achievement of better performance with superior electrical properties, which are of fundamental and applied importance for advanced engineering applications such as electrical power transport, communication signal transmission, and other electrical systems.

---

## Methods

Materials
The chemical vapor deposition (CVD) process was conducted for graphene growth. Before in-situ grown graphene, in order to remove the surface impurities, the Cu foils with a thickness of 25 μm were immersed in acetone for ultrasonic cleaning. Cold rolled polycrystalline Cu foils with a thickness of ~25 μm and conductivity of ~97.08% IACS were placed in a tube furnace and annealed at 1273 K for 20 min in a hydrogen/argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the methane, which served as the carbon source, was introduced for graphene deposition. The graphene growth was holding on 20 min with methane and hydrogen gasses flow of 3 sccm and 10 sccm, respectively. Then the Gr–Cu foils were rapidly cooled down to room temperature within 30 min. The photograph of Gr–Cu foil, microstructure of Cu matrix and graphene, as well as Raman analysis, are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. The as-deposited Gr–Cu foils were stacked layer by layer in a graphite die, and the sintering of bulk Gr–Cu composite was carried out using a hot-pressing furnace with a vacuum of ~6×10−2 Pa. The uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa was applied at 400 °C and held for 3 h, followed by continually heating to 900 °C for 2 h, and then naturally cooled down to 100 °C in the furnace.

Hot extrusion was conducted after heating at 750 °C for 40 min. A Φ13 mm bar was obtained, and the surface oxidized layer was removed. Subsequently, the Gr–Cu bar was continually cold-drawn at room temperature. The true strain is defined as ε=ln(A0/A), where A0 and A are the cross-sectional area before and after cold drawing. The whole cold drawing process was carried out at ambient temperature without any intermediate annealing. The annealing process was carried out in a tube furnace at 300–500 °C for 1 h under a tube furnace under a hydrogen/argon atmosphere. The Cu wire was manufactured using the same raw materials and method.

Structure characterization
The sintered sample, different diameter Gr–Cu wires, and annealed Gr–Cu wires were polished. The TEM samples containing the DD and ND cross-sections were prepared by FEI Helios 5CX focus ion beam (FIB). TEM analysis was performed on a FEI Talos F200× at a voltage of 200 keV and a spherical-aberration-corrected TEM (Spectra 300) at a voltage of 300 keV. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis was conducted on a GAIA3 SEM. Transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD) was performed on a Mira3 SEM. A nanoMEGAS PED was used to perform the high-resolution grain orientation observation.

Raman characterization
Raman characterization was conducted using a Renishaw inVia Qontor Raman spectroscopy system with a laser wavelength of 532 nm and laser power of 25 W. Calibration with a standard silicon sample was carried out before testing. The spectral resolution was of ≤1.0 cm−1. Further correlative SEM-Raman characterization was carried out on a TESCAN RISE-MAGNA with a laser wavelength of 532 nm.

Mechanical and electrical conductivity testing
The tensile tests of Gr–Cu wires with a diameter of more than 0.5 mm were performed on an Instron 5966 universal testing system with a strain rate of 5×10−4 s−1 at room temperature. A TH-8203S servo control computer tensile testing machine was used for the wires with a diameter of less than 0.5 mm. Five tests were performed to obtain the statistics.

The electrical conductivity tests for wire and foil samples were performed on a test system developed by us based on the Kelvin bridge method (Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25). For the wire sample, a current source meter (Keithley 2601B) was used to provide current, and a nanovoltmeter (Keithley 2182A) was used for measurement of the voltage difference. The diameter of the wire was determined using a laser diameter gauge with an accuracy of ±(0.00012+0.03%D), and we also conducted repeated measurements on a SEM. In addition, a TX-300A resistivity meter was also used to verify the result of the same sample. For the foil sample, a resistivity measurement system based on the van der Pauw method was used (Supplementary Fig. 25). Moreover, known-conductivity pure copper wire (100% IACS) was used for the calibration of the test system.

Synchrotron μ-XRD
In order to examine the lattice strain of the cold-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu wires, the synchrotron μ-XRD experiments were conducted in transmission mode on the BL15U1 beamline of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). The main experimental parameters are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. The Gr–Cu wires were thinned using a FIB to enhance the transmission rate. The instrument calibration was performed using a standard CeO2 powder sample. The measured 2D Debye-Scherrer patterns were processed using the Fit2D software28.

In situ TEM shear deformation
TEM sample was prepared in a GAIA3 SEM. The grain boundary, including the Cu–C interface, was determined based on the backscattered image, and a local region containing the Gr–Cu interface was fabricated to ensure the Gr–Cu interface was located in the middle area. The in-situ TEM shear was carried out inside a Titan-ETEM field-emission gun TEM, equipped with an INSTEM S-MT TEM holder under displacement control mode at 2 nm/s. Throughout the shear deformation process. All in situ experiments were recorded in real time by a camera at a shooting interval of ~1 s.

In situ TEM heating testing
In situ TEM heating testing was carried out in a Talos F200X TEM using a FEI heating holder for low-magnification observation and a JEM-ARM300F spherical-aberration-corrected TEM using a DENS solution DH30-4M-JU heating holder for high-magnification microstructure observation. The heating rate was set to 1 K/s with holds at 473 K (15 min), 573 K (15 min), 623 K (15 min), and 673 K (15 min). The temperature measurement of the holder was calibrated by measuring the temperature curve and Raman spectrum of the standard sample. All in-situ heating processes were recorded in real time.

First principles calculations
The first-principles calculations were conducted using the QUANTUM ESPRESSO package53, based on the density functional theory (DFT) with the optimized Norm-Conserving Vanderbilt Pseudopotential54,55. The unit cell of FCC copper was considered using the experimental equilibrium lattice constant of 3.60 Å. The atomic coordinates of the optimized computational models corresponding to the four strain states are provided in the Supplementary Data. The energy cutoff of 100 Ry was chosen for the wavefunctions. The electron charge density was calculated by the Methfessel-Paxton method with a smearing parameter of σ=0.02 Ry (4). To consider the Gr/Cu composite, we constructed the systems by following two steps. Firstly, we relaxed the bulk Cu with fixed different lattice parameters to simulate the effect of a hydrostatic pressure. Then, we cleave the Cu(111) surface to construct the heterojunction of Cu(111)@Gr with two different stacking orders. The heterojunctions are optimized with fixed Cu position and lattice parameters, while the C atoms are fully relaxed. The hydrostatic pressure is simulated by change the crystal parameters and fully relaxed the atomic positions, where the Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) quasi-Newton algorithm was used. Phonon dispersion curves were calculated based on the density functional perturbation theory (DFPT)56, where a denser 20×20×20 k-point and a 5×5×5 q-point grids were employed for the EPC calculations. The phonon line width is calculated by
γqv = 2πωqv ∑ij ∫BZ d3k |gqv(k,i,j)|2 × δ(εqv − εF)δ(εk+q,j − εF) (1)
Here, gqv(k,i,j) is the electron-phonon matrix and is defined as
gqv(k,i,j) = ( 2M ℏ ωqv )1/2 ⟨ψi,k | dVSCF / du^qvξ^qv | ψj,k+q ⟩ (2)
where ψ is the wavefunction, V is the Kohn-Sham potential, û is the atomic displacement, and ξ̂ is the phonon eigenvector. The total EPC constant can be evaluated by
λ = ∑qυ λqυ = 2 ∫ α2F(ω) / ω dω (3)
where α2F(ω) is Eliashberg spectral function and is defined as
α2F(ω) = 1 / (2πN(EF)) ∑qυ γqυ / (ℏωqυ) δ(ω − ωqυ) (4)

MD simulations
The MD simulations were performed in the isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble with a constant pressure of 1 atm and temperature maintained at 300 K, utilizing the large-scale atomic/molecular massively parallel simulator (LAMMPS)57. The interatomic interactions in the Cu–C system were modeled using the Embedded Atom Method (EAM) potential for Cu–Cu pairs58, the Adaptive Intermolecular Reactive Empirical Bond Order (AIREBO) potential for C–C interactions59, and the Morse potential for Cu–C pairs43, with a 20 ps NPT ensemble relaxation phase incorporated in the simulation. A polycrystalline composite model was constructed following the multigrain architecture methodology60 proposed by Li et al., with graphene layers embedded at GBs. Periodic boundary conditions were implemented in all spatial dimensions. The simulation employed a timestep of 1 femtosecond (fs) and a strain rate of 5×108 s−1. Atomic configurations were visualized and structurally characterized using the Open Visualization Tool (OVITO)61. The MD trajectories of Cu and Gr–Cu corresponding to the initial and final configurations are provided in the Supplementary Data.

Statistics and reproducibility
Each electrical conductivity value was obtained from three independent samples, and the measurement for each sample was repeated five times. TEM microstructure in Fig. 1f was obtained from the region (marked by a white box) in Fig. 1e, and one experiment was conducted because the regions with similar microstructural characteristics are very common in the EBSD map in Fig. 1e. TEM microstructure analysis in Figs. 2a, d and 3a–d was repeated from three independent samples. Moreover, the typical HRTEM microstructure, such as twins and distorted nanolayer, exists along the boundary or interface, and the distorted lattice was highly reproducible in the three independent experiments.

### Reviewer 1

This paper discussed the improvement in electrical conductivity of copper through the addition of graphene and deformation of composite followed by annealing. It discusses the microstructure of the composite and hypothesizes the mechanisms for enhanced conductivity. While the approach for enhancing conductivity is interesting, I would recommend publication of this paper only after significant information is added on the material and synthesis approach, the measurement approach, material evolution, first principles calculations and clarifying some language concerns.
1. Pg 2, Ln 33 – 34: Please clarify why an increase of 10% conductivity is equivalent to effect of an external high pressure of about 10 gigapascals – this is not clear anywhere in the paper.
2. Pg 3, Ln 58 – 61: The authors discuss recent papers where Gr/Cu composites were manufactured showing enhanced electrical conductivity under different conditions, and state that these strategies do not alter intrinsic electrical conductivity of the metal matrix, and still rely on their structural integrity, namely single-crystallization and high purity – which is inherently not true. All the papers reviewed here have added Gr to Cu, meaning they are not relying on single crystallization and high purity. This discussion has to be changed for accuracy.
3. However, what is more surprising is the authors are doing exactly the same as the papers they cite as ref 11-14 - which is adding Gr to Cu in their study. This leaves the reviewer rather confused because the authors’ premise is to change the intrinsic electrical properties of Cu, but they are doing so by adding Gr(?). The premise (Pg 3, Lines 73 – 76) then seems contradictory and therefore unclear – is the hypothesis to add Gr to Cu so that Gr acts as highly conductive channel? Or is it increasing the defects in Cu alone? And if the measurements are made in the annealed condition, how does that justify the existence of “local giant stresses”? The paper seems to be written for increasing defects in Cu, especially the DFT model, but the results are shown for Gr. Please clarify the hypothesis further.
4. Pg 3, Line 85: What was the purity of copper and/or alloy composition? What trace elements were present? Since all these components affect conductivity prior to and after straining the composite, it is crucial to present this data.
5. Pg 3, Line 84 – please provide the graphene content incorporated. This is important information know as the electrical conductivity of a copper/graphene composite is assessed. Studies have shown that conductivity of such composites is a strong function of graphene content.
6. Pg 5, Line 123: For such a measurement to hold, it is crucial for the authors to discuss the uncertainty in measurement afforded by the system, as well as its calibration of a known-conductivity sample by the system. Given that the authors present conductivity at various sample diameters, uncertainty in measurement for each of these conditions must be presented, along with the temperature of measurement. There are error bars for the conductivity in Fig 1g – are these referring to standard deviation from repeated measurements? What measurement standards were used? What was the gage length used? All these contribute to uncertainty in measurement and need to be discussed. Since the Methods section states that the conductivity tests were performed by the authors on the system they developed (Pg 20, Ln 541), it is not clear what purpose the certification documents in SI are serving – please clarify.
7. Pg 4, Figure 1g: How was the Cu wire manufactured? Was it made using the same Cu that was used in the synthesis of the Gr-Cu wire? Several details are missing to assess the viability of these results.
8. Pg 5, Line 124: Pure copper has a range of electrical conductivities depending on its purity – for example, 6N copper is ~103% IACS in electrical conductivity. Thus, it becomes important to discuss the electrical properties of the copper that was used in the study for its relevance to the mechanism.
9. In all microstructure images, while the scale bars are evident, it is not clear what these bars represent. No text is evident around them to understand what they are – please correct this.
10. The authors discuss lattice distortion at multiple locations in the paper. Since the material is a composite (Copper and graphene are immiscible as they note in Line 208, Pg 9), then there are two lattices to consider. However, the language in the paper doesn’t specify which lattice is being considered at specific locations. Please clarify this information for further clarity.
11. There are no images of the graphene species in the extruded or drawn/annealed samples. There is also no discussion of the fate of evolution of the graphene films to whatever becomes of them in the extruded condition. There is an assumption that they become flakes? How and why is not discussed at all. Please provide this information. There is a discussion of ‘nanolayers’ but it is not clear if this refers to graphene or copper. For example, Fig 2f refers to a nanolayer along grain boundary – is this graphene? Is the chemical species carbon? The diffusion region seems like it might be oxide at the interface. Did the authors perform EDS? Significant clarifications are required to reduce confusion in these areas. Similarly, in Fig 3 A-d, it seems like the authors are showing two nanolayers formed along the grain boundaries – are these graphene? The image 3f seems to suggest so, but it is not at all clear either in the caption or in the paper text. Same issue with Fig. 3g and 3h – what layers are being discussed here – what chemical species? All of these chemical species, and material structure needs to be clarified.
12. Pg 9, Ln 206 – 209: how did the authors exclude any possible contribution from impurities? This is challenging to assess with the information presented here, since no information on the feedstock purity has been provided. Additionally, if the copper and copper/graphene wires were made from foils that were extruded, there should be oxides present significantly, as the lower size of the copper foils without graphene will have a native passivation layer. Was this removed prior to manufacturing the wires? How? Please clarify. Also, unless the extrusion and drawing were performed in a closed environment, the wire will have oxides – please clarify how this is not evident in the results.
13. If the first principles calculations are comparing an FCC copper cell and another cell, also copper, but with changed crystal parameters and fully relaxed atomic positions (Pg 21, Ln 577 – 583), then yes, the electron-phonon coupling will be lower in cell with relaxed atomic position. But that is not a true representation of the Gr/Cu system whose properties the authors are trying to explain – rather it is only a part of the composite system, the copper part. This therefore cannot be used to explain the conductivity improvements in Gr/Cu composite, as the authors are attempting to do in Pg 13 Ln 325, and in comparison, with Figure 4b with experimental measurements from cold-drawn and annealed Gr-Cu composite system. The DFT model will need to be evolved to accommodate Gr species as well.

There is a growing body of literature that shows that in composites such as those manufactured in this work, the graphene plays an important role in providing high velocity pathways for phonons and electrons. Please interpret your results in that context, since the paper is not discussing the role of graphene beyond pinning grains, which may not sufficiently explain conductivity improvement.
15. The language in the paper will benefit from grammar and spell check. The issues are too numerous to point out in this review unfortunately but are significant to make it challenging to understand the authors’ arguments at places. Kindly consider editing closely for clarity.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

High electrical conductivity is crucial for electrics, electronics, communications. Eliminating defects such as grain boundaries and impurities is a primary approach to enhancing electrical conductivity in metals. Although reducing electron-phonon interaction can further contribute to electrical conductivity, only a marginal enhancement is obtained by imposing external pressure even high up to gigapascal. Here we report a contrary strategy to transforming defects into conductive benefits, by forming abundant defects of severely distorted lattice via heterogeneous interface-assisted plastic deformation in metal (copper). Such lattice distortions are generated under a non-extreme condition, and cause internal giant local stress significantly suppressing electron-phonon coupling and thus reducing phonon-caused electron scattering. Consequently, a striking bulk electrical conductivity of >110% IACS is obtained in the copper at room temperature, which is equivalent to the effect of an external high pressure of about 10 gigapascals. Our work provides an extendable approach for developing high-performance metal conductors.

---

## Introduction

Electrical energy is the main form of energy transport and conversion. The development of high-performance conductor materials has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of systems and devices, reduce energy consumption, and increase integration and power density. Taking an example, the electrical conductivity of interconnects exceeding that of pure copper can effectively improve signal transmission rate, reduce bit error rate, and chip power consumption1–5. According to Matthiessen’s rule, electron scattering caused by phonon and lattice defects, including vacancies, grain boundaries (GBs), impurities, and dislocations, collectively deteriorates electrical conductivity in metals1,6–8. To minimize the deleterious effects of the above electron scattering factors on electrical conductivity, a multitude of methods have been employed, such as increasing lattice integrity and inhibiting grain refinement, as well as purification.

Copper is the most widely used metal conductor material owing to its high conductivity and low cost. However, a very limited increment in the electrical conductivity of Cu has been achieved since the International Annealed Copper Standard (IACS, electrical conductivity of Cu is 100% IACS) was established in 1913. For example, electrical conductivity is less than 103% IACS in oxygen-free Cu with a purity as high as 7N-level, and ~110% IACS in Cu single crystal without GBs9,10. In recent years, some explorations have shown the potential in improving electrical conductivity to a higher level by forming composites either in bulk or on surface2,11–13, and the enhancement of electrical conductivity was mainly attributed to the doping effect, reducing electron scattering on the Cu–C interface, enhancing thermal heat dissipation, etc. But most of the above strategies do not alter the intrinsic electrical conductivity of the metal matrix.

Essentially, the intrinsic electrical conductivity of some phase is dominated by its electronic structure and energy band, which can be influenced by applying external fields, including force, temperature, and magnetism, etc., leading to some strategies such as strain engineering and band engineering14–17. For example, the compression-shear stress on diamond changed charge redistribution and softened phonon, resulting in the production of robust superconductivity18. Regarding metals, it was proved that applying pressure on Cu can suppress electron-phonon coupling (EPC) and thus improve its electrical conductivity, but a very limited increment by 2% was achieved19 when subject to high pressure, even up to 2 gigapascal (GPa). Moreover, in most cases, these benefits are not integrated as intrinsic properties of the materials, and they disappear as the applied fields are removed.

Contrary to the conventional wisdom of eliminating structural defects, we proposed introducing nanolayers of severely distorted copper lattice at GBs in nanograined Cu to act as highly conductive channels by means of suppressing electron-phonon interaction strength and reducing phonon-caused electron scattering. The local giant stress is caused by accumulated copious strain energy upon cold drawing (ε≈12) and subsequent annealing-induced anisotropic expansion due to the thermal expansion coefficient (TEC) mismatch between the Cu matrix and strained graphene at GBs. Additionally, it has high thermal stability (at least up to 773K), and no external extreme fields are required to maintain it.

---

## Results

Fabrication and ultra high electrical conductivity
To obtain sufficient deformability and grain refinement to the nanoscale simultaneously, we incorporated trace graphene (Supplementary Note 1, about several tens of parts per million in volume fraction) at GBs to assist plastic deformation of coarse-grained Cu20. The ultimate nanograined Cu wires were obtained through a sequential process involving in-situ growth of graphene on Cu foils (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1), laminated structure assembling, hot-pressing molding, hot extrusion, and cold drawing, followed by a subsequent thermal annealing treatment in the final step (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2). Such trace graphene at GBs enables Cu exceptional plastic deformability, i.e. the extruded bar (diameter d=13 mm) can be continuously cold drawn to wires (d<0.03 mm) without intermediate thermal annealing (corresponding to a strain of ~12, Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). Because of the constraint role of graphene at GBs, Cu samples containing trace graphene (Gr–Cu) have stronger ability on grain refinement and higher thermal stability than that without graphene inside (Fig. 1b, f, Supplementary Fig. 4, and Supplementary Fig. 5). After thermal annealing treatment, with the same diameters (d≈0.4 mm), grain size coarsened up to ~50±13.4 μm in the pure Cu wire (Fig. 1b), much larger than the value of ~0.72±0.21 μm in the Gr–Cu wire (Fig. 1c). As the drawing process continued, nanograined structures were formed and retained in the final cold drawn Gr–Cu wires and annealed Gr–Cu wires, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12 and Fig. 1d–f).

We compared the electrical conductivities of Gr–Cu wires and Cu wires prepared using the same raw materials and method (Fig. 1g and Supplementary Fig. 6). For pure Cu wires, as expected, their electrical conductivities decrease gradually with increasing strain, and slightly recover upon thermal annealing treatment. In contrast, the electrical conductivity of the Gr–Cu wires remains almost unchanged in the whole process of cold drawing, and witnessed drastic increases after thermal annealing treatment, with a certified exceptional electrical conductivity larger than 110% IACS (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Fig. 7), which is more than 10% higher than that of pure Cu. It is worth emphasizing that, contradictory to the conventional belief that as the grain size is refined to nanometer scale, the electrical conductivity will significantly decrease21,22, the electrical conductivity inversely increases with decreasing grain size in the plastically deformed Gr–Cu here (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 8). Our findings strongly suggested that grain refinement not always decreases electrical conductivity, which contradicts the notion established in conventional materials.

While Ag is well known as the best electrical conductor among all the metals, the Gr–Cu here shows comprehensive advantages over Ag as indicated by the expanded area in the performance radar chart (Fig. 1j). Ag has higher electrical conductivity than Cu, but Cu is used in much larger quantities because Ag is too expensive. The Gr–Cu material provides an attractive choice with electrical conductivity higher than Ag but price around Cu. Moreover, pure Cu has a higher current-carrying capacity than Ag, and incorporating graphene will further improve this performance23,24, indicating higher power and safety in applications. Additionally, the density of Gr–Cu is almost the same as that of pure Cu, about 85% that of Ag, implying direct benefit for lightweighting in practical devices and systems. In many applications, high electrical conductivity and high mechanical strength are often required simultaneously, but methods used to strengthen metals generally also cause a pronounced decrease in electrical conductivity1. Fortunately, the Gr–Cu material has both higher electrical conductivity and mechanical strength than either Cu or Ag, which provides a pathway to develop high-performance metal conductors.

Nanostructure formation and lattice distortion
In the as-sintered Gr–Cu sample, a micro-laminated structure was observed, and the lamellae thickness of ~25 μm is close to the thickness of the raw Cu foils and the as-prepared Gr–Cu foils (Supplementary Fig. 9), implying that the inter-lamella graphene inhibited across-lamella grain coarsening in the process of hot-pressing sintering. By subsequent hot extrusion and multi-pass cold drawing, the few-layer graphene at GBs was thinned and further dispersed via shear-induced interlayer sliding (Supplementary Fig. 10 and Supplementary Video 1), and plays the role of inhibiting dynamic recovery and recrystallization against plastic deformation. As a result, the lamellae were continuously thinned and finally refined to the nanoscale (Supplementary Fig. 11).

As the diameter of the Gr–Cu wire reached ~50 μm (corresponding to a strain of ~11), the average lamellar thickness is about 100 nm (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 11). Such graphene-assisted deformation has a prominent ability for grain refinement, and differs from the conventional refining mechanism dominated by dislocation slip in pure Cu under moderate deformation conditions25,26. The kernel averaged misorientation (KAM) map (Fig. 2b) suggests high misorientation within grains in the as-drawn Gr–Cu wire (d≈50 μm), i.e., a high density of dislocations was accumulated, and copious strain energy was stored inside after cold drawing. Nanotwins are also observed as penetrating through the Cu lamellae with a twin/matrix thickness of ~10 nm (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 12).

Thermal annealing treatment is the only process resulting in the remarkable enhancement of conductivity, and we compared microstructure change in the annealed Gr–Cu wire (d≈50 μm) (Fig. 2d–g). The nanolaminated structure remained after annealing, and the grains slightly coarsened to an average grain size of 175±138 nm. As a noticeable difference from the as-drawn sample, the annealed sample shows much weaker intragranular misorientation, while strong misorientation concentrates along the lamellar boundary or the Gr–Cu interface (Fig. 2e). These observations imply that the stored strain was redistributed upon thermal annealing. Under high-resolution TEM (HRTEM), we found nanolayers with a clear contrast exist along boundary or interface (Fig. 2f), and corresponding geometrical phase analysis (GPA) shows obvious lattice strain in the nanolayers of Cu matrix (Fig. 2g). Carefully examination of the interplanar spacing of the Cu(111) in the distorted region was changed by ~10% (indicated by the blue and yellow box in Supplementary Fig. 13d).

Furthermore, we estimated the lattice strain by performing synchrotron X-ray micro-diffraction (μ-XRD) (with a wavelength of 0.563 Å and a spot size of ~5 μm) on both the as-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu wire samples (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 14). The 1-D patterns integrated from the Debye-Scherrer rings27,28 are shown in a 2θ angle range from 10° to 35°. The diffraction peaks at the 2θ angles of 15.5°, 17.9°, 25.5°, 29.9°, and 31.3° correspond to the (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222) planes of Cu, respectively. The as-drawn sample has diffraction peaks with a typical symmetrical profile, indicating homogeneous microstructure and strain distribution (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Fig. 15). Usually, thermal annealing treatment can reduce lattice defects and promote crystallinity, resulting in sharper diffraction peaks29,30. However, some abnormal changes were observed in the μ-XRD patterns of the annealed Gr–Cu sample. After annealing, while the diffraction peak intensities increase significantly, asymmetrical broadening at varying degrees takes place in the peak profiles, typically as shown at the foot of the peaks at low diffraction angles. More μ-XRD patterns with varying features of peak broadening and also some extra peaks are shown in Supplementary Fig. 15. We excluded any possible contribution from impurities to such unusual changes in diffraction patterns because (1) graphene and Cu are immiscible with each other, (2) no oxides were detected by checking peak positions and using electron energy loss spectroscopy. Moreover, the thermal annealing treatment was carried out in an inert atmosphere, and μ-XRD was performed on the polished fresh surface. Hence, we believe that such asymmetrical broadening of peaks was caused by anisotropic strain31 and thus inhomogeneous lattice distortion of the copper lattice in the annealed Gr–Cu wires. Based on the Scherrer equation, we can roughly estimate the type and degree of such observed lattice distortion according to the peak positions, either expansion or compression of interplanar spacing32,33. Lattice compression distortion was mainly reflected by the asymmetrical broadening on the right foot side of some diffraction peaks, with a typical broadening width of about 1~2° for 2θ, indicating that the corresponding interplanar spacing was compressed by ~5% (see Supplementary Note 3 for further details).

Microstructure evolution inducing local strain
To explore the microstructure evolution and formation of lattice distortion during annealing, we conducted in-situ heating experiments in TEM. The low-magnification TEM images revealed that the nanolaminated structure was thermally stable during in-situ heating (Supplementary Fig. 16 and Supplementary Video 2). Closer observations in HRTEM (Fig. 3a–d) show some meaningful details on microstructure evolution. In the randomly selected nanolamella (about 50 nm in width) in the TEM specimen cut from the as-drawn Gr–Cu wire, dense strain moiré fringes were observed in the lamellae before heating34,35. As the heating temperature increased, the strained zone became narrower gradually, and the fringes in the middle region of the nanolamella disappeared ultimately, which seems like the strain was concentrating towards GBs on two sides upon heating. As revealed by HRTEM, two nanolayers with clear contrast and compressive strain (εxy) formed along the GBs on both sides (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Video 3), which is consistent with the features of microstructure and nanolayers as observed in the ex-situ annealed Gr–Cu samples (Fig. 2f).

We also conducted Raman measurements of graphene in the interface to estimate the interfacial stress (Fig. 3e). We observed a slight blue shift of the Raman G peak after sintering (without deformation), and a larger shift to higher wavenumbers in the as-extruded Gr–Cu sample (with an extrusion ratio of 9.5 and a strain ε≈2.2). Raman peak position can be used as the index of strain state in graphene; a significant red shift of ~14.2 cm−1 per 1% strain for Raman G peak was observed in graphene under uniaxial tensile strain36. In contrast to the tensile strain, the reported in-plane biaxial compression-induced blue shifts37 of the Raman G peak for the graphite or graphene vary from 4.1 to 4.9 cm−1·GPa−1. Compared to pristine graphene38 or our graphene transferred from Gr/Cu foil to silicon substrate, the blue shift of the Raman G peak in the as-extruded sample is estimated to be around 30 cm−1 in our work. Thus, it can be approximately calculated that the compressive stress caused a shift of the G peak of 6.1–7.3 GPa. It is reasonable to expect that even more significant Raman shifts and thus actual stress much larger than 8 GPa in the annealed Gr–Cu wires (the strain ε as high as 12 in the wire with d<0.03 mm), although it is challenging to further collect Raman spectra for the highly dispersed graphene in the Cu matrix.

This interfacial stress induced by the TEC mismatch between the severely strained graphene and Cu matrix was elucidated in Fig. 3f. Upon elevating temperature during sintering and annealing, along the direction parallel to the nanolamella, graphene contracted due to its negative TEC in-plane39 while the Cu matrix oppositely expanded. Subsequently, graphene tends to expand while Cu tends to shrink, resulting in the formation of graphene wrinkles (described as ripples or folds) during the cooling process. The interfacial compressive stress was partially released by forming folds or ripples40,41, while the majority of the compressive stress was still retained, resulting in a biaxial compressive stress on the Cu matrix. In the other direction, perpendicular to the nanolamella, graphene itself expanded and also constrained the expansion of the Cu matrix, thus leading to a uniaxial compressive stress. Consequently, a multi-directional compressive stress formed near the Cu–C interface, which is consistent with that reported in the graphene/Cu micro-laminated composites42. However, only in the drawn Gr–Cu wire does such a compressive stress effect contribute to a substantial increase in bulk electrical conductivity. Firstly, copious strain energy was accumulated in the process of cold drawing, and graphene was highly strained, resulting in a larger compressive stress generated at the Cu–C interface. Additionally, the proportion of the strain-affected area becomes large enough as the Cu lamellae are refined to the nanoscale. For instance, the width of the distorted nanolayer ranged from 5 to 20 nm for the nanolamellae with a thickness of ~50 nm in Figs. 2f and 3d. Such microstructure evolution and strain accumulation can well explain the strain-dependent enhancement of electrical conductivity (Fig. 1g, h).

Giant stress in the annealed Gr–Cu wire was also confirmed by severe lattice distortion of copper, as shown in the atomic-scale images of the nanolayer (Fig. 3g, h) collected by high-resolution high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) imaging in an aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM). As shown in Fig. 3g, we clearly identify a distinctive torsion of the (111) planes. In addition, a typical expansion of (200) interplanar spacing increased by ~27%, from ~1.80 Å to ~2.29 Å in the distorted nanolayer was observed (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 18), which was confirmed by some extra peaks around 2θ of ~14° in the μ-XRD patterns (inset, Supplementary Fig. 16). Further first-principles calculations indicated that such a large lattice expansion requires local stress of several tens of GPa. We have also conducted molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the maintaining effect of graphene on the mechanical properties of the graphene-reinforced copper composites and stable interfacial bonding (Supplementary Fig. 19). The results show the remarkable increase in the tensile strength due to the hindering effect on the dislocations. Especially, comparing with the microstructure at a strain of ~0.5, the microstructure at a strain of ~0.7 was kept stable without interfacial separation. Additionally, the detachment phenomena are less likely to occur under compressive loading43. Thus, based on the above experimental and MD results, interfacial compressive stress was induced and kept without interfacial separation.

Suppression of EPC
Strain-tuning electrically conductive performance was further elucidated by conducting first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 20). The EPC constant λ and Eliashberg spectral function α2F(ω) were obtained. The calculated λ is 0.124 for copper under unstrained conditions. This is in good agreement with the previously reported value41 of 0.14. As the compressive strain increased to 2%, 5%, and 10%, the corresponding calculated λ decreased to 0.113, 0.095, and 0.07, 8 respectively. We also noticed that the spectral functions were shifted to higher frequencies after applying strain, and the intensities of the peaks were reduced, resulting in weakening the scattering effects on electrons. Thus, according to the calculated Eliashberg spectral function α2F(ω) and frequency-dependent EPC λ(ω), we can infer that the electron-phonon interaction strength was reduced after applying strain19,44. As the lattice strain can be determined to be ~5% from the μ-XRD diffraction patterns, a pressure of ~30 GPa was required to achieve a similar lattice strain in the above DFT-calculated hydrostatic pressure. Similar compressive strain increasing the conductivity was also confirmed using experimental tests and simulated calculations in the copper/graphene composites45. Besides, it was recently proposed that the electrical resistivity decreases in aluminum and copper wires upon pressuring each metal19 (Supplementary Fig. 21d). If the graphene-wrapped nanograin in the Supplementary Fig. 21c is analogized to a copper wire, its compressive stress state is similar to that reported in the literature19. Moreover, similar experimental and simulation results on compressive stress suppressing EPC to enhance the conductivity of Au have also been reported in our recent work46. Theory calculations reveal that ~60% increment of electrical conductivity can be achieved at ~30 GPa for the metals of silver and gold47. Göran Grimvall48 systematically investigated the effects of electron-phonon interaction (λ) on the electronic properties and electrical performance, and concluded that λ for the noble metals is well within the approximate limits 0.07–0.24 (Cu), 0.05–0.25 (Ag), and 0.07–0.26 (Au). Besides, a similar recommended value for the Cu, Ag, and Au of ~0.14 was given. Moreover, the ratio of resistivity to temperature (ρ/T) can be used to describe the scattering of conduction electrons by thermal vibrations, and the trend of Cu is close to that of Ag49. As shown in Fig. 2d, 20% nanostructured grains remained in the annealed Gr–Cu wire due to the Cu–C interface. Consequently, we estimated the average electrical conductivity of ~112% IACS according to the rule of mixtures. This is in close agreement with our measurement results of ~110% IACS for the bulk Gr–Cu samples. For comparison purposes, we also accommodated graphene into the DFT model and carried out the corresponding calculations in Supplementary Fig. 22. The calculated λ is 0.171 for the Gr–Cu composite model under unstrained conditions. As the compressive strain increased to 5%, the corresponding calculated λ decreased to 0.137. The variation is about 0.034, which is generally close to that of the FCC copper cell. Considering the distribution of graphene in the Gr–Cu wires and the interfacial compressive stress, graphene was employed as a medium to cause internal giant local stress, resulting in significantly suppressing EPC and enhancing electrical conductivity. Thus, the DFT model of the FCC copper cell could be more suitable to simulate the experimental results.

This suppression of EPC was further confirmed by the measured temperature-dependent resistivity curves of cold-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu composite wires from 3 to 300 K using the physical property measurement system (PPMS) (Fig. 4b). The resistivity of the cold-drawn and annealed Gr–Cu wires at 293 K was 1.67 μΩ·cm and 1.54 μΩ·cm, respectively. This is roughly consistent with the results measured using macroscopic samples in Fig. 1g. As shown in Fig. 4b, the electrical resistivity of the two samples decreased linearly with the temperature down to 100 K. Subsequently, the two curves showed nonlinear trends below 100 K until close to horizontal. It is found that the residual resistivity (ρ0) of the as-drawn sample is 1.75±0.05×10−2 μΩ·cm, which is close to the values (0.51×10−2 μΩ·cm) of the oxygen-free copper (OFC) and the values (0.33×10−2 μΩ·cm) of the single-crystal copper (SCC) in the literature10,21. The residual resistivity values (6.75±0.04×10−2 μΩ·cm) of the annealed sample are larger than those of the as-drawn sample. According to Boltzmann transport theory, the residual resistivity caused by defect scattering is temperature independent50,51. It suggests that the annealed sample contains more defects than that in the cold-drawn sample. Furthermore, the measured temperature coefficient of resistivity at 293 K was ~6.7×10−11 K−1 for the cold-drawn Gr–Cu sample. This matches well with the value of 6.8×10−11 K−1 for the oxygen-free high conductivity (OFHC) Cu52. As a comparison, it was ~5.9×10−11 K−1 for the annealed Gr–Cu sample, which is ~12% lower than that of cold drawn sample. These results indicate that the EPC was suppressed at moderate temperature in the annealed Gr–Cu sample due to the distorted nanolayer.

Our observations indicate that abundant GBs with a distorted lattice in the nanograined Cu enable an exceptional electrical conductivity and also comprehensive properties outperforming those of bulk Ag. Such a property enhancement differs fundamentally from that of the traditional strategies, lying in structural integrity and phase purity. Reduction in the electron–phonon interaction strength by introducing lattice distortion through conventional plastic deformation can be emerged as an intrinsic property of materials, making not only the effect more significant but also extreme external conditions unnecessary, such as high pressure. Our findings also demonstrate that grain refinement (a typical method to enhance strength) does not always lead to a decrease in electrical conductivity, combining strengthening with a second phase (graphene here), which provides an effective approach to enhance electrical conductivity and mechanical strength simultaneously, which has been a long-standing challenge in materials science. Such a strategy, achieving many objectives at one stroke, could also be feasibly applied to many other 2D-material/metal systems, particularly toward the achievement of better performance with superior electrical properties, which are of fundamental and applied importance for advanced engineering applications such as electrical power transport, communication signal transmission, and other electrical systems.
